title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Introduction
content: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum . The disease progresses through primary, secondary, and tertiary stages, each defined by characteristic clinical manifestations. Asymptomatic infection is classified as latent syphilis.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Introduction
content: Without adequate treatment, syphilis may result in neurological and cardiovascular complications. Infection during pregnancy can lead to congenital syphilis, with substantial morbidity and mortality. Therefore, early detection is essential to prevent disease progression and associated adverse outcomes.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Introduction
content: Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) assays are nontreponemal serologic tests traditionally used to screen for active syphilis and monitor response to therapy. Owing to limited specificity, reactive nontreponemal results require confirmation with treponemal-specific assays, including the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test, Treponema pallidum enzyme immunoassay, T pallidum particle agglutination test, and automated chemiluminescent immunoassays. [1]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Etiology and Epidemiology
content: Syphilis is a prevalent STI worldwide. The disease is caused by T pallidum , a motile spirochete bacterium for which humans are the only natural host. According to the World Health Organization, 5.6 million cases of syphilis were reported globally in 2012. [2] An estimated 10 to 12 million new cases occur annually.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Etiology and Epidemiology
content: The risk of acquiring syphilis increases with a greater number of sexual partners. Since the late 1990s, a resurgence of syphilis has been observed among homosexual men. Increasing rates of coinfection with other STIs, including HIV, have also been reported. [3] Early-stage syphilis has additionally been identified with greater frequency among heterosexual men and women in the United Kingdom. Congenital syphilis is a significant global health concern, with an estimated 500,000 to 1 million new cases reported each year. [4]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Pathophysiology
content: T pallidum enters the body via microtrauma, most frequently through mucous membranes. Sexual intercourse constitutes the primary route of transmission, including oral sex and oral-anal contact. Transmission is most likely when primary and secondary syphilitic lesions are present. Less commonly, infection occurs via blood transfusions or organ transplantation from donors with active syphilis. Clinical classification divides the disease into primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary stages.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Pathophysiology
content: Primary syphilis exhibits the highest transmissibility and is typically characterized by a single painless chancre, although multiple lesions occur in a minority of cases. [5] A macule forms at the inoculation site, progressing to a papule that subsequently ulcerates. The incubation period from inoculation to lesion development ranges from 2 to 3 weeks. Lesions heal spontaneously in approximately 5 weeks if untreated.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Pathophysiology
content: Secondary syphilis is characterized by a maculopapular rash affecting the palms and soles bilaterally. Bacteremia may occur, accompanied by fever and fatigue. Untreated secondary syphilis typically resolves within 3 to 6 weeks. Recurrence occurs in approximately 25% of patients within a year. [6]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Pathophysiology
content: Latent syphilis follows, in which individuals remain asymptomatic but demonstrate positive serologic results. Latent infection is subdivided into early and late stages. According to the WHO, early latent syphilis corresponds to infection of less than 2 years’ duration, whereas late latent syphilis refers to infection exceeding 2 years. [7] Approximately 35% of patients with late latent syphilis progress to tertiary syphilis, which is characterized by chronic end-organ damage several years after inoculation. Manifestations include neurosyphilis, gummatous syphilis, and cardiovascular syphilis.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Pathophysiology
content: In neurosyphilis, T pallidum invades the brain and spinal cord 5 to 20 years after primary infection, primarily affecting the dorsal columns. Tabes dorsalis, or spinal cord syndrome, presents with ataxia, loss of vibration and proprioception, urinary and fecal incontinence, and absent limb reflexes, and may include psychiatric disease and dementia. Gummatous syphilis develops as granulomatous lesions of bone or skin 3 to 12 years after primary infection. Cardiovascular syphilis is characterized by aortitis, or inflammation of the aortic wall, predominantly involving the proximal (ascending) aorta approximately 15 to 30 years after primary infection. [8] [9]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Pathophysiology
content: Approximately one-third of infants born to infected mothers are affected by congenital syphilis. Fetal infection occurs via transplacental transmission during pregnancy, most likely within the first 2 years of maternal infection. Spontaneous abortions and stillbirths occur in one-third of syphilitic pregnancies. Clinical manifestations in affected infants include hepatosplenomegaly, abnormal dental development, nasal chondritis (“snuffles”), deafness, and craniofacial abnormalities. Congenital syphilis is preventable with antenatal screening and treatment during pregnancy. Parenteral penicillin is the treatment of choice for syphilis at any stage.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure
content: The RPR test requires serum as the preferred specimen, although plasma is acceptable. An optimal volume is 2 to 4 mL, with a minimum of 2 mL required for analysis. Each specimen must be clearly labeled with the patient’s full name, date of birth, and the date and time of collection. [10] Specimens should be centrifuged promptly to separate serum or plasma from cellular components. Separation must occur as soon as possible to prevent hemolysis or sample degradation. Once separated, serum or plasma may be stored frozen at –20 °C or colder if testing is delayed.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure
content: Clinical or relevant medical history should accompany the requisition to aid in the interpretation of results. Any precipitates present must be removed by centrifugation before testing. Specimens exhibiting moderate to gross hemolysis, lipemia, bacterial contamination, improper or missing labeling, or insufficient quantity will be rejected.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Diagnostic Tests
content: Serological testing is the primary method for diagnosing syphilis. Two categories of serologic assays exist: nontreponemal (nonspecific) and treponemal (specific). Nontreponemal tests include RPR, VDRL, and toluidine red unheated serum test, with RPR and VDRL used most frequently. Treponemal assays include T pallidum particle agglutination, chemiluminescent immunoassay, and T pallidum enzyme immunoassay. Diagnosis may also be achieved via dark-field microscopy of genital lesion samples in patients with primary or secondary syphilis. [11]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Diagnostic Tests
content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends nontreponemal reagin tests as first-line screening for syphilis infection. The primary nontreponemal assays are RPR and VDRL. The RPR test demonstrates 86% sensitivity in primary syphilis, 73% sensitivity in latent syphilis, and 100% sensitivity in secondary syphilis.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Testing Procedures
content: RPR card tests are nontreponemal flocculation assays that detect reagin antibodies in plasma and serum. The RPR antigen mixture consists of cholesterol, nonspecific cardiolipin, and lecithin. A 0.05 mL drop of serum is applied to a circle on the testing card for each assay and spread evenly within the circle. A drop of the prepared antigen suspension is added to each specimen. Testing cards are rotated in a humidified chamber at 100 rpm for 8 minutes, then manually rotated and examined macroscopically under a light source. Agglutination indicates the presence of immunoglobulin M or G antibodies to lipoidal antigens.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Testing Procedures
content: Titers of reactive samples are initially determined at 1:1, and serial dilutions in phosphate-buffered saline are performed to establish an endpoint titer, typically up to 1:16. A 1:50 nonreactive serum–phosphate-buffered saline solution is used for titers exceeding 1:16. The endpoint titer corresponds to the highest dilution at which aggregation remains visible. RPR titers of at least 1:32 indicate increased risk for neurosyphilis. [12]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Interfering Factors
content: False-negative results in nontreponemal testing arise from several factors. The primary cause is testing during the early stages of primary infection. Additional contributors include reduced antibody reactivity due to HIV coinfection and the conduction of the test during late-stage syphilis in untreated patients. The “prozone effect” may explain some false-negative results, occurring when excessively high concentrations of antibodies or antigens impair immune complex formation. Manual RPR testing is also vulnerable to subjective human error, as the interpretation of results depends on the observer and may vary among individuals.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Interfering Factors
content: False-positive results occur in association with intravenous drug use, HIV infection, hepatitis B infection, and autoimmune diseases. In such cases, titers are frequently 1:8 or lower, potentially prompting unnecessary invasive testing and treatments, including unwarranted lumbar punctures and associated adverse effects. [13] Since RPR antigens are natural constituents of human cells, the assay cannot distinguish whether detected components originate from bacterial antigens, damaged host cells, or both. False-positive nontreponemal results occur in 1% to 2% of patients in the United States. Consequently, confirmation with a specific treponemal test is required to minimize the risk of false-positive diagnoses.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings
content: RPR results are interpreted as reactive or nonreactive (see Image . Reactive and Nonreactive Rapid Plasma Reagin Card Demonstration). Repeat testing or reporting of an “indeterminate” result may occasionally be required, necessitating further evaluation. Reactive nontreponemal results must be confirmed with treponemal assays. Patients with concurrent HIV infection are advised to undergo serologic testing for syphilis every 3 months for 1 year and again at 2 years posttreatment. Patients without HIV are recommended to follow up with serologic testing at 6 and 12 months.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings
content: Syphilis is a reportable STI in the United States. Patient demographics, sex, ethnicity, and age are recorded for each case. The CDC collects data on reportable STIs through the National Electronic Telecommunications System for Surveillance. Certain cases undergo further investigation by local health departments, with additional risk factors, including men who have sex with men and HIV infection, also documented. Reported cases of primary and secondary syphilis in the United States have increased markedly over the past 15 years. Following a historic decline to 2 cases per 100,000 in 2001, the reported rate tripled to 8.7 cases per 100,000 by 2016. [14]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Clinical Significance
content: RPR serves as a first-line test for screening syphilis infection, playing a critical role in preventing disease progression and associated sequelae. Complications of untreated syphilis include potentially fatal cardiac and neurologic conditions. Use of RPR in pregnant women enables early detection and treatment, preventing transplacental transmission and congenital syphilis. Beyond diagnosis, RPR testing monitors treatment response: reactivity typically declines following therapy and can detect reinfection. Positive serology usually appears within 3 to 6 weeks after exposure.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Clinical Significance
content: High rates of syphilis coinfection occur among individuals with HIV in certain populations. Syphilis infection may also facilitate HIV transmission. Screening with RPR, particularly during primary and secondary stages, allows public health and clinical providers to reduce HIV acquisition among uninfected individuals and identify and link HIV-infected individuals lacking medical care to appropriate management.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Quality Control and Lab Safety
content: RPR testing is considered a relatively inexpensive and simple procedure. However, significant variability exists between laboratories. A 2009 report by Gupta et al documented a 58.7% variation in RPR results across 138 serology panels in 26 laboratories. Contributing factors included delayed testing, suboptimal laboratory temperature, use of different RPR card tests, and inconsistent interpretation of results. Accurate RPR testing requires standardized resources and strict adherence to guidelines. Essential requirements include refrigeration for antigen storage, monitoring of laboratory temperature and humidity, a reliable light source, and an uninterrupted electricity supply. Antigens are sensitive to sunlight, freezing, and thawing. Properly trained personnel are necessary to ensure the correct interpretation of RPR results.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Quality Control and Lab Safety
content: Automated RPR testing is available and can accommodate larger sample volumes while reducing reader subjectivity. Despite these advantages, automated nontreponemal assays have demonstrated inconsistent results when used to monitor treatment response. Quality control and laboratory safety for both manual and automated RPR testing depend on structured practices that incorporate internal quality control, external quality assessment, and compliance with the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 15189:2022 and the College of American Pathologists (CAP) accreditation standards. [15]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Quality Control and Lab Safety
content: Internal quality control involves the routine use of positive, weak-positive, and negative controls at defined frequencies, such as with each manual test run or automated test according to the manufacturer’s schedule for automated systems, to verify reagent integrity, instrument performance, and operator technique. [16] All control outcomes must be documented, reviewed, and trended over time. Deviations from acceptable limits require immediate corrective action and suspension of patient result reporting until resolution. [17] Participation in external quality assessment or proficiency testing programs provides an independent evaluation of laboratory performance. Proficiency testing samples must be processed identically to patient specimens, and any unacceptable results require thorough investigation, documentation, and use in improving laboratory processes and staff competency. [18]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Quality Control and Lab Safety
content: Laboratory safety measures, including consistent use of personal protective equipment, safe handling and processing of serum or plasma, prevention of aerosol generation during centrifugation, and proper waste disposal, maintain a secure testing environment and preserve specimen integrity. These practices collectively comply with ISO 15189:2022 standards for risk management, method verification, equipment calibration and maintenance, document control, and ongoing competency assessment. These practices also satisfy CAP requirements for comprehensive quality control documentation, participation in proficiency testing, validated procedures, and traceable corrective and preventive actions. [19] [20]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Syphilis prevention and early detection depend on strong interprofessional collaboration. Increasing screening demands have necessitated expanded roles for pharmacists, nurses, and other healthcare professionals to improve access and reduce community transmission. In the United States and the United Kingdom, pharmacists participate in point-of-care screening using dried blood spot testing kits. These kits allow patients to self-collect fingerstick specimens while trained pharmacy staff conduct the assay. Results are available within 15 minutes, with reported sensitivity and specificity exceeding 99%.

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Pharmacists trained in patient counseling, risk assessment, and specimen handling play a critical role in identifying high-risk individuals, including participants in needle exchange or opioid substitution programs, while maintaining biosafety standards to prevent blood-borne exposures. Pharmacy-based screening, although accessible and effective, requires structured training, adherence to ethical practice, and integration with public health systems. [21] Task shifting has strengthened screening capacity, with nurses performing syphilis testing in clinics and community programs across the United States, the Netherlands, and Australia. Nursing responsibilities include patient education, risk assessment, sample collection, and linkage to care, enhancing early detection and supporting continuity of care for vulnerable populations. [22]

title: Rapid Plasma Reagin -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Collaborative models integrate physicians, pharmacists, nurses, laboratory professionals, and public health teams through shared protocols, structured communication, and coordinated follow-up. Recognizing the expertise of each team member and reducing hierarchical barriers enables healthcare systems to provide safer, more efficient, and patient-centered syphilis screening. This interprofessional approach improves access to diagnosis, reduces disease transmission, and enhances patient and public health outcomes.
